title: {{NAME}}'s Perfect Kick
moral: Believing in yourself is the first step to doing something amazing.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a determined young boy with wavy red hair and green eyes, wearing a green-and-white striped soccer jersey, black shorts, and green soccer cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The morning of the big match, {{NAME}} couldn't eat his breakfast.

"What if I miss?" he asked his mum.

"Then you try again," she said simply, and tucked a note into his sock.

At the ground, {{NAME}} looked at the goal. It seemed enormous. The whole world seemed to be watching. He could feel his legs going wobbly, right down to his green cleats.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} got his first chance early in the second half. The ball rolled to his feet, the goal was open, and he swung his leg back —

The shot went wide. Way wide. It bounced into the corner flag.

{{NAME}}'s face went hot. He stared at the grass. He wanted to disappear into it.

Then he remembered the note in his sock. He bent down and unfolded it. It said: "Kick with your heart, not just your foot. Love, Mum."

pages.content:
In the final minute, the score was tied. {{NAME}}'s teammate crossed the ball perfectly — it arced through the air and dropped right at his feet.

Everything went quiet. Not real quiet. The crowd was roaring. But inside {{NAME}}'s head, it was peaceful and clear.

He thought of his mum. He thought of every practice, every rainy afternoon, every time he'd stayed an extra ten minutes after everyone else went home.

He kicked.

pages.content:
The ball flew straight and true — right into the top corner of the net.

The crowd erupted. His teammates piled on top of him, laughing and shouting his name. The coach pumped his fist. The goalkeeper just stared.

{{NAME}} lay at the bottom of the pile, looking up at the blue sky, laughing harder than he had in months.

"That's the one," he said to no one in particular.

pages.content:
That night, {{NAME}} had mud on his knees and grass stains on his jersey. He didn't want to wash either of them.

He put the note from his mum in his top drawer — the one he saved for important things.

His legs ached in the best possible way as he climbed into bed. He thought about the shot. The way it had felt — not like kicking a ball at all, but like letting go of something heavy and watching it soar.

He closed his eyes, and was asleep before his mum had even turned off the light.
